briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Michigan Weed Finds Its Footing While D.C. Speeds Toward Schedule III
briefs.top: Michigan operators are adapting fast to the 24% wholesale tax — cost-sharing deals, hospitality buildouts, and out-of-state expansion are keeping growth alive even as Lansing's revenue math comes up short. Nationally, the DEA rescheduling case has reached closing arguments, Compass Pathways is racing toward a Q4 psilocybin filing, and M&A is accelerating — all pointing toward a friendlier 2027 for plant-touching and psychedelic operators alike.

local.text: A new dispensary called Blue Sky Cannabis Co. is now open in downtown Ann Arbor next to Spores Cafe, a popular mushroom cafe — a fresh sign of retail confidence right in THE STICKY TRAP's backyard.

JARS Cannabis, the Michigan-based chain, is buying its way into a much bigger footprint out west, acquiring Sonoran Roots and its eight Ponderosa brand dispensaries, a deal that will make the homegrown operator the largest dispensary chain in Arizona.

Fields Cannary, a Muskegon development, is targeting a fall opening for its retail cannabis dispensary, with a full-service restaurant to follow — a hospitality-forward format that pushes Michigan retail further than most dispensaries have gone.

Wholesale-tax pain is easing on two fronts: Michigan weed prices have leveled out after three months of steady increases, with the average ounce down to $59 in April from $62 in March, and Rize, which operates three Upper Michigan locations, has managed to sustain growth by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers, splitting the tax burden rather than absorbing it alone.

The 24% tax is underperforming — four months in, Michigan has collected less than $34 million, less than a third of the roughly $105 million the tax would need to generate each quarter to hit its $420 million annual target — and that shortfall is now driving real political traction: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James says the tax 'drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge, and has already fallen far short of revenue projections,' and pledges to work to repeal or sharply reduce it.

national.text: The federal rescheduling fight is entering the home stretch: the week of August 24 saw the federal rescheduling case reach its closing-argument stage, with the DEA trying to discredit nearly all opposing witnesses in its post-hearing brief as legal experts flag testimony on currently accepted medical use as pivotal — a sign the Schedule III decision is finally close.
national.source: Cannabis Business Advisors / Cannabis Business Times

national.text: Psychedelics keep clearing hurdles: the FDA granted Compass Pathways' rolling NDA review request and awarded COMP360 a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher for treatment-resistant depression, and the FDA has scheduled a public hearing on the therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs for September 14, 2026, building toward what could be the first-ever approved psilocybin therapy.

President Trump commuted the sentences of more people with marijuana convictions as his administration continues to consider federal cannabis rescheduling, adding to the momentum toward clemency and reform.

M&A is heating up again: Minneapolis-based MSO Vireo Growth is acquiring fellow operator Planet 13 Holdings in an all-stock merger, extending one of the cannabis industry's most aggressive buying sprees, and will operate about 265 retail stores and dispensaries across 15 states after the deal closes, positioning it as one of the largest U.S. cannabis operators by store count.

Hemp got breathing room, not a reprieve: the chamber voted to back the Senate's plan to delay the federal government's ban on certain hemp-derived cannabinoid products until Dec. 11, and Trump signed off, buying operators time to shape the next round of regulation.
